rules.statement: The token revocation endpoint must respond 200 OK to every authenticated request, whether the token was revoked, unknown, or of a type that can't be revoked. It must never return 400 or 404 for an unknown or non-revocable token.
rules.why: RFC 7009 requires this leniency so that the endpoint does not become an oracle that tells real tokens apart from fake ones.
rules.check: Look for revocation handlers that return an error status, or a different response, when the token is not found, is already revoked, or is an access token.

rules.statement: In the token revocation endpoint, treat a missing `token` parameter as the only hard request error, and return 400 with `invalid_request` for it.
rules.why: RFC 7009 makes `token` required. Every other outcome must look the same to the caller so that token state is not revealed.
rules.check: Check that a missing or empty `token` produces invalid_request, and that no other token-state condition produces a distinct error.

rules.statement: Before revoking a persisted grant or refresh token, verify that its owning client ID matches the authenticated client. If it doesn't match, do not revoke it, and still return 200.
rules.why: RFC 7009 section 2.1 says only the client a token was issued to may revoke it. Without this check, a client that obtained another client's token value could revoke it.
rules.check: Look for revocation code that sets a revoked marker (such as RevokedWhen) without comparing the grant's ClientId to the authenticated client's ID.

rules.statement: Require client authentication before any token revocation logic runs.
rules.why: Only a registered client may reach revocation, and ownership can only be checked against an authenticated client.
rules.check: Look for revocation endpoints that call the revocation logic before authenticating the client, or without authenticating it at all.

rules.statement: Treat revocation of a stateless self-contained JWT access token as an accepted no-op. Do not add per-token server state, such as a denylist lookup, on the resource-server validation path unless that is explicitly required.
rules.why: A stateless JWT can't be invalidated without server state, and adding a lookup on every call defeats the purpose of stateless tokens. Short access-token lifetimes limit the exposure instead.
rules.check: Look for revocation code that tries to persist or denylist JWT access tokens, or for access-token validation that adds a store lookup for revocation state.

rules.statement: Keep OAuth endpoint providers thin. The provider authenticates the client and parses the form into a typed request, then delegates to a mediator command handler that holds the business logic.
rules.why: This follows the established OAuth endpoint and mediator conventions, so every endpoint has the same structure, for example matching the token endpoint.
rules.check: Look for endpoint provider classes that contain revocation, grant, or other business logic inline instead of sending a command through the mediator.
